hints: Start from the titre by calculating moles of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ used, remembering to convert $15.20 \text{ cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the balanced equation $2\text{MnO}_4^- : 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2$ to convert moles of manganate(VII) to moles of ethanedioic acid in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ aliquot.
Remember the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ portion is only one quarter of the $100.0 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, so scale up before converting to mass with $M_r = 90$ and then to a percentage of $40.0 \text{ g}$.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate(VII) actually delivered**
You have concentration times volume. Convert the titre to $\text{dm}^3$ first: $$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0200 \times \frac{15.20}{1000} = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ This is the amount that reacted with the acid in that one flask.

Jump across the equation to ethanedioic acid**
Look at the coefficients: $$2\text{MnO}_4^- + 6\text{H}^+ + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So $2$ mol manganate reacts with $5$ mol acid. Multiply by $5/2$: $$n(\text{acid in }25.0 \text{ cm}^3) = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{5}{2} = 7.60 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Scale from aliquot to whole extract, then to percentage**
The $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ came from a $100.0 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, so multiply by $4$: $$n(\text{total}) = 7.60 \times 10^{-4} \times 4 = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ With $M_r(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2)=90$: $$m = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \times 90 = 0.2736 \text{ g}$$ Then: $$\% = \frac{0.2736}{40.0} \times 100 = 0.684\%$$

Final answer: $n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0200 \times 15.20/1000 = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$
$n(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2)$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \times 5/2 = 7.60 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$, so in $100.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$\text{mass} = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \times 90 = 0.274 \text{ g}$; $\% = 0.274 \times 100/40.0 = 0.684\%$

hints: Think of the standard way to replace both $-\text{OH}$ groups of a carboxylic acid by $-\text{Cl}$ without using aqueous conditions.
walkthrough:
Recognise the functional group change**
You are going from $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{ClOC-COCl}$. Each $-\text{OH}$ is swapped for $-\text{Cl}$ to make an acyl chloride. The classic reagents for this are thionyl chloride, $\text{SOCl}_2$, or phosphorus chlorides $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$

hints: Recall what happens when an acyl chloride meets an alcohol and when it meets a primary amine, focusing on what replaces $\text{Cl}$ in each case.

For K, count atoms in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ plus $\text{ClOC-COCl}$ and think how two amide links can join to close a six membered ring of formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$.
walkthrough:
Build J from methanol**
Methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, acts as a nucleophile toward each $\text{COCl}$ group. $\text{Cl}$ leaves as $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{OCH}_3$ attaches. With two $\text{COCl}$ groups you get the diester: $$\text{ClOC-COCl} + 2\text{CH}_3\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3 + 2\text{HCl}$$ This matches $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$.

Build K from 1,2-diaminoethane**
$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ has two $\text{-NH}_2$ ends. Each end can attack one $\text{COCl}$ group to form an amide link, $\text{-CO-NH-}$. Because the diamine is the right length, the two ends bridge the two carbonyl carbons to close a ring. You lose $2\text{HCl}$ and form a six membered cyclic diamide containing $\text{O=C-C=O}$ at the top and $\text{HN-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH}$ around the bottom.

Final answer: J is dimethyl ethanedioate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3$
K is the cyclic diamide: a six-membered ring $\text{-CO-CO-NH-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-}$ with two $\text{C}=\text{O}$ groups adjacent.

hints: Look at the symmetry of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to decide how many different carbon signals the solvent itself should show.
Use the Data Booklet ranges to match $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{O}$ to the peaks near $\delta$ 15 and $\delta$ 65.
walkthrough:
Use symmetry to predict solvent peaks**
Picture $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. The molecule is symmetric through the $\text{O}$, so the two $\text{CH}_3$ carbons are identical and the two $\text{CH}_2$ carbons are identical. Expect just two peaks from the solvent.

Assign with Data Booklet shifts**
Carbon attached directly to oxygen is deshielded, so $\text{CH}_2\text{-O}$ appears downfield around $\delta$ 65. Alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ appears upfield around $\delta$ 15. In the spectrum the peaks at $\delta$ 15 and $\delta$ 65 are therefore the ethoxyethane solvent, leaving the peak near $\delta$ 162 for L.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3$ carbons at $\delta$ 15; $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ carbons at $\delta$ 65

hints: Count how many peaks remain for L after removing the solvent peaks and think what that tells you about equivalence of its four carbons.
walkthrough:
Read equivalence from peak count**
After assigning the two solvent peaks, only one peak near $\delta$ 162 is left, yet formula $\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$ contains four carbons. One signal means all four carbons experience exactly the same chemical environment. L must be very symmetric with no overall dipole, consistent with a cyclic symmetric oxide.
Final answer: L shows only one carbon-13 peak, so all four C atoms are in the same environment, molecule is highly symmetric.

hints: Identify M from its formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$ and single peak at $\delta$ 162 as the parent diacid.
Compare formulas: N ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$) is M plus $\text{CH}_2$, O ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$) is M plus $2\times\text{CH}_2$, suggesting stepwise methylation.
Use the peak counts: O shows two peaks ($\delta$ 53 and 160) for two equivalent ester groups, N shows three peaks for one acid plus one ester group.
walkthrough:
Pin down M as the diacid**
M has formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$ and only one carbon signal at $\delta$ 162, typical of $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in an acid. That fits $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ where both carbonyl carbons are equivalent. It also makes sense that heating N or O with aqueous acid gives M by acid hydrolysis of esters.

Read N as the half ester**
N is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$, exactly M plus $\text{CH}_2$ from one $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. Its spectrum has three peaks: $\delta$ 53 for $\text{OCH}_3$, plus two different carbonyls at $\delta$ 160 and 162 for ester $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and acid $\text{C}=\text{O}$. So N is $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-CO}_2\text{H}$ with no symmetry.

Read O as the diester**
O is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$, M plus $2\times\text{CH}_2$ from two methanols. It shows only two peaks: $\delta$ 53 for the two equivalent $\text{OCH}_3$ carbons and $\delta$ 160 for the two equivalent ester carbonyls. So O is symmetric $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3$.

Final answer: M is ethanedioic acid, $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$
N is monomethyl ester, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-CO}_2\text{H}$
O is dimethyl ester, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3$ (same as J)

hints: Combine the facts that L has formula $\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$, one carbon environment, no dipole, and reacts with methanol to give acid plus esters, to infer a double anhydride ring.
walkthrough:
Assemble a structure that explains all the clues**
L contains only C and O, $\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$, with all C equivalent and no dipole. Reaction with $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ opens it to give the diacid, monoester and diester, which is classic anhydride behaviour. Joining two $\text{-CO-CO-}$ units with two bridging $\text{O}$ atoms gives a symmetric six membered ring: $\text{O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-}$ closed back to the start. Every carbonyl carbon is identical, giving one $^{13}\text{C}$ peak, and the symmetric ring has no overall dipole.
Final answer: L is the cyclic dianhydride: six-membered ring $\text{-O-CO-CO-O-CO-CO-}$ with all $\text{C}=\text{O}$ equivalent.
